prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on this shortlist of a new measurement capability opening new physics. The magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating thousands of atoms at once, and this has brought systematic uncertainty and instability to the 1e-18 level, reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL). The result is measured and reproducible rather than projected: relativistic geodesy at millimetre scale, sensitive tests of constant variation and dark-matter couplings, and a formal roadmap toward redefining the second. The attribution is as clean as any on the list. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength concept and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group drove the accuracy, stability and many-body clock work that set the frontier. Seven of eight members ranked this ballot and all seven proposed the same two names, which is notable, but I rest my case on the experimental evidence and not on that convergence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is field overlap and novelty. Ye already shares the 2005 prize for frequency combs and precision spectroscopy, Wineland shared the 2012 prize for ion-based quantum measurement and clocks, and a committee may feel that precision time and frequency has been honoured often. A second reservation is timing: the redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened, and the ultimate payoff in geodesy and fundamental-physics searches is still mostly promise. I do not think these are decisive, because the lattice-clock step is a distinct and well-demonstrated advance (many-atom interrogation with a lattice free of first-order shifts) that is not covered by the combs or ion-clock citations, and because the performance is already confirmed. It is still a real objection and I would want the committee to address it openly.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of precision atomic physics opening fundamental tests, and notes that Hall, Haensch and Wineland are already recognised and not credited here.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment, and as a fellow atomic physicist I think her point about the comparisons (millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, constant-variation limits) is the right way to frame the case. Where I would add a qualification is that agreement between two atomic-physics members should not be mistaken for breadth of support. We should test whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes really leave room, and the citation should stay tightly on the lattice and magic-wavelength advance. I would also ask whether the stability and many-body clock work of Ye's group is distinguishable enough from the 2005 citation to defend, and I believe it is.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first for a clean, general Z2 mechanism with protected edge states. He ranks the lattice clock fourth, noting that redefinition of the second is pending and so there is a case for waiting.
responses.response: I take the topological case seriously, and the HgTe experiment by Molenkamp is the kind of decisive demonstration I respect. My difficulty is that the credit is the hardest on the list: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is outside the credited names, Mele and Hasan force a choice among four, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree. The clocks' performance is already established and is not contingent on a metrological decision, and the formal redefinition will follow the evidence rather than create it. Waiting would risk honouring a roadmap step instead of the discovery.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a natural continuation of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, with Blais for theory and Wallraff and Schoelkopf for experiment.
responses.response: I ranked circuit QED third and regard it as a genuine technique that opened a field. But I read the 2025 prize as a reason for caution, not a reason to proceed: the committee just recognised the superconducting-circuit platform, and giving the same community a second prize within a year looks heavy. Credit is also incomplete without Girvin, whose role in the 2004 proposal the credited names cannot capture, as Johansson himself notes. I would keep circuit QED as a strong later candidate and as my first alternative. I also recognise that his proximity to the field makes his view informed, and I note his own flagged conflict.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, valuing the pairing of the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction with the 2018 experiment, and describes the field as robust and timely.
responses.response: The theory-plus-experiment link is persuasive and the replication across groups is real. My concern is maturity, which Mehlig, Olsson and Danielsson also raise: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled, and the discovery is under a decade old. I also notice that Cao, as first author of the decisive experiments, falls outside the credited names, which weakens the experimental credit. The clocks, by contrast, have two decades of independent confirmation. I would not rule moire matter out, but I think it benefits from a few more years.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as a km3-scale detector that opened neutrino astronomy, and ranks the clocks third.
responses.response: IceCube is a real instrumental achievement and I respect its detector development. The issue I would press is the one Pearce himself raises: the allocation among Halzen, Spiering and Karle is debatable given the AMANDA and Baikal precursors, and source identification is still developing. I would want to see whether the credit can be justified from the experimental record before comparing it with a well-defined two-person clock prize. I do not dismiss it and have no strong view against it, but the attribution problem puts it behind the clocks for me.

uncertainties: How heavily the committee should weigh the earlier 2005 (combs, Ye) and 2012 (ion clocks) prizes against the distinctness of the lattice-clock step.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or simply a downstream consequence of an already established result.
I am less able to judge the astroparticle (IceCube, Higgs) and condensed-matter (topological, moire, TMR) attribution questions from my own expertise and rely on colleagues.
Whether a second, distinct part would add value; a shared prize with circuit QED or Hubbard simulation would exceed the three-person limit with these credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the lattice-clock candidates (Katori, Ye). I have worked in atomic physics and quantum memories at Lund, and spent a year during my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder (JILA), the institution where Ye works. This is a scientific lineage connection only, not a collaboration with the credited laureates, but I flag it for the record. I am also part of the WACQT leadership, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers (Johansson), and would be more cautious on circuit QED for that reason.
